analysis.one_liner: Restricts bulk sales of defaulted government-backed mortgages, forcing investor buyers to work with homeowners before foreclosing.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 30, 2026 with four Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate Banking Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a homeowner with an FHA, Fannie Mae, or Freddie Mac loan stops paying, the government agency or company backing the loan can sell it in bulk to investors, who often then foreclose. This bill would set rules for those sales: the borrower must first get a fair shot at a loan modification, must be notified 90 days ahead by certified mail, and buyers must offer help at least as good as government loss-mitigation programs. It would also require that most foreclosed homes go to owner-occupants, nonprofits, or affordable rentals instead of investors, and create a "first look" window letting regular buyers and community groups purchase foreclosed FHA homes before investors can.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners behind on FHA, Fannie Mae, or Freddie Mac mortgages whose loans could be bundled and sold to investors; renters and neighborhoods that would see more foreclosed homes sold to occupants or affordable uses instead of bulk investors; and nonprofits, land banks, and local governments, which would get first claim on these loans and properties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners facing foreclosure on government-backed loans

how_it_helps.text: Before an FHA loan can be sold to investors, the homeowner must exhaust all government loss-mitigation options, and the servicer must send the borrower and any owners of record clear written notice by certified and first-class mail at least 90 days before the sale, describing what protections remain available.

Investors who buy the loans must offer modification and deferral programs with terms and fees at least as favorable as FHA or Fannie/Freddie guidelines, and if a buyer breaks those rules, the borrower can use that failure as a defense against foreclosure.

For homes the investor takes through foreclosure where keeping the owner in the home was not possible, at least 75% must go to an owner-occupant, a nonprofit or government that commits to that outcome, or an affordable rental (rents capped at 30% of income for tenants at or below 100% of area median income, with a guarantee that vouchers and benefits like Social Security count as legal income).

The bill creates a 'First Look' program for FHA-foreclosed homes: owner-occupant buyers, pre-qualified nonprofits, and government agencies get an exclusive window to buy at or below fair market value before any investor bid.

Loans cannot be sold while the borrower is in a forbearance plan or within 90 days of one ending, and the FHA cannot sell at all unless it has determined no other measure can keep its insurance fund above minimum capital requirements.

Buyers are barred from using contract-for-deed, rent-to-own, or land installment contracts (arrangements with a history of stripping equity from low-income buyers) unless the buyer is a nonprofit, and must maintain vacant properties and keep paying local property taxes until the property is transferred.
Purchases would come with four years of quarterly loan-level reporting, public semiannual reports to Congress, and a fair-lending analysis to detect discriminatory outcomes from the sales.
Direct FHA loan sales would be limited to municipalities, land banks, and nonprofits working in affordable housing, and the FHA must give these buyers priority in regular sales.

analysis.who_pays: Investors that buy pools of defaulted government-backed mortgages, which would pay more or earn less under mandatory loss mitigation, notice rules, resale restrictions, and penalties including losing the loans without compensation. Mortgage servicers face new notice and documentation duties. If the restrictions lower what buyers will pay for loan pools, the FHA insurance fund and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could recover less on sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill concedes the protections make loans worth less: it requires that prices for direct sales 'reasonably reflect the costs of complying' with the new rules. If pools of defaulted loans fetch less, the FHA insurance fund and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac recover less, and the FHA fund's health is backstopped by the insurance premiums homeowners pay.

By cutting the pool of eligible buyers and the profits they can expect, the rules could mean fewer bidders for distressed loans, so some delinquent loans could take longer to resolve — though the bill responds by restricting when sales can happen at all.
The rules apply only at the point a government agency or enterprise sells a loan; they would do nothing for homeowners whose loans were already sold to investors under the old rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are substantial and concrete: notice, mandatory modification offers, enforceable foreclosure defenses, and a shift of foreclosed housing stock toward owner-occupants and affordable rentals. The real cost is that investors will pay less for loan pools, and the FHA fund and the housing enterprises may take smaller recoveries — a cost ultimately shared by FHA-insured borrowers through premiums and taxpayers through the enterprises. The bill also tries to contain that cost by letting the FHA sell only when its fund needs it. The trade-off favors homeowners and neighborhoods, at a price paid largely by investors and modestly by the funds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee on January 30, 2026, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the Preserving Homes and Communities Act of 2026 in the Senate on January 30, 2026, joined by Senators Smith, Wyden, Schumer, and Merkley as cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in its action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No rules have changed, so investors that buy pools of defaulted government-backed mortgages continue operating under the current, less restrictive rules; no homeowner has gained anything yet either.

for.name: Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no opponent has acted on the record; so far the bill's support is entirely Democratic, with all five Senate backers being Democrats.

industries.industry: Investors in distressed-mortgage loan pools (hedge funds and private equity)
industries.note: These firms buy bundles of government-backed loans from homeowners who have stopped paying, at deep discounts, and profit through foreclosure, resale, or renting. The bill cuts into that model: loss mitigation must be exhausted first, buyers must offer modifications without fees, 75% of foreclosed homes must go to owner-occupants or affordable uses, and repeat violators can lose the loans without compensation.

Servicers would have to send certified and first-class mail notice 90 days before any sale, document the borrower's loss-mitigation history in that notice, and comply with post-sale servicing duties that can be used as a foreclosure defense if broken.

The enterprises lose the freedom to shed defaulted and re-performing loans in bulk on any terms: sales would require nonprofit/government priority, borrower notice, and buyer protections. In exchange they get clearer rules, and restricting sales keeps more troubled loans in their own workout programs, where borrowers get federal loss-mitigation options.

industries.industry: Community housing nonprofits, land banks, and municipalities
industries.note: They get priority as purchasers of FHA and enterprise loan pools, exclusive access to direct loan sales, and a seat in the First Look window for foreclosed FHA homes, with FHA pre-approval standards for participation.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills die in committee without a hearing, and this one has seen no committee action since referral. With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to reach the floor this Congress; the realistic path is that it sits until the session ends, though its sponsors have re-introduced similar bills across past Congresses and could do so again.
